title: Molecular Design of Fluorinated Ester Electrolytes via Skeleton Regulation Enables Aggressive Cathode Chemistries in 5V‐Class Fast‐Charging Lithium‐Ion Batteries
content:
The rational design of the MTFP solvent via skeleton regulation optimizes the distance between the trifluoromethyl substituent and the carbonyl group, balancing Li+ coordination with oxidative stability. Unlike mediocre fluorinated solvents, MTFP effectively sustains 5 V‐class LNMO cathodes, suppressing oxidative decomposition and transition metal dissolution to ensure robust battery performance.








ABSTRACT
Lithium‐ion batteries can deliver higher energy densities when using high‐voltage cathodes such as LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 (LNMO), yet their practical application is hindered by the catalytic nature of high‐voltage cathode materials which usually cause electrolytes decomposition. Although the utilization of fluorinated carbonates as electrolyte solvent considerably inhibited the parasitic reaction at cathode side, the irrational fluorination often leads to the sluggish Li+ transport which finally causes poor rate performance. Here, we design a family of trifluoromethyl‐substituted carboxylate esters as electrolyte solvents. We found that the spatial arrangement between the ‐CF3 and the carbonyl group in these fluorinated esters is critical for regulating the electrolyte solvation structures. A short distance (α‐substitution) severely weakens the solvating power of the solvent, resulting in a substantial decrease in ionic conductivity, whereas an extended separation (γ‐substitution) compromises the oxidation resistance against high‐voltage cathodes. Only the trifluoromethylation at the β‐position yields optimal solvent (methyl 3,3,3‐trifluoropropionate, MTFP) that can simultaneously meets high‐voltage and fast‐charging requirements of LNMO||Gr cells when pairing with fluoroethylene carbonate and 1 M LiPF6. In such electrolyte, the Ah‐level LNMO||Gr pouch cells deliver 78% capacity retention at 6C charge/discharge rate (13.2 mA cm−2), and stably operate over 300 cycles at the high rate of 3C.

title: Rational Solvent Fluorination Design for Solvation Regulation Enabling Stable Interfaces in High‐Voltage Li‐Ion Batteries
content:
In this work, we systematically investigate a family of fluorinated‐diethyl carbonate (fluorinated‐DEC) molecules which are readily synthesized on large scales to work as the electrolyte solvents. Selected positions on DEC are functionalized with various numbers of trifluoromethyl groups through iterative tuning, to reach a balance between oxidative stability and the Li+ coordination environment.








ABSTRACT
Fluorinating electrolyte solvents is an effective strategy to enhance the interfacial stability of lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) under high‐voltage conditions, where severe interfacial side reactions typically undermine the long‐term performance. However, the influence of both the number and positional arrangement of fluorinated groups on solvation structure remains poorly understood. In this work, we systematically investigate how trifluoromethyl group number and substitution position in diethyl carbonate (DEC) derivatives affect Li+ solvation behavior. It is revealed that the introduction of a DEC‐based solvent with symmetric two trifluoromethyl groups tends to regulate the solvation structure enriched with anions and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). This optimized solvation structure facilitates the formation of a robust cathode‐electrolyte interphase derived from both anions and FEC. Consequently, Ni‐rich LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 cathodes with a high loading mass of 10.5 mg cm−2 achieve stable cycling at 4.6 V, retaining 80% of their capacity after 300 cycles. These findings provide fresh insights into the rational design of fluorinated solvents for high‐voltage LIBs.

title: Molecularly Aligned Insoluble Nanoaggregates for Ah‐Level Aqueous Zinc‐Ion Batteries
content:
A molecularly aligned electrolyte is designed by incorporating insoluble ligands that assemble into nanoaggregates via π−π stacking in aqueous electrolytes. Upon adsorption, these insoluble molecular nanoaggregates substantially enhance the water‐repelling capability for both electrode‐electrolyte interfaces, enabling stable Ah‐level aqueous zinc‐ion batteries.








ABSTRACT
Achieving stable Ah‐level aqueous zinc‐ion batteries (AZIBs) remains a critical challenge due to severe water decomposition and dendrite growth. Conventional aqueous electrolytes adopt soluble ligands to stabilize the interfaces, yet these species are insufficient to isolate interfacial water contact owing to their intrinsic hydrophilicity. Herein, we design a molecularly aligned electrolyte (MAE) that incorporates insoluble ligands in aqueous solutions to stabilize both electrodes. By utilizing the π−π stacking between benzylideneacetone (BA) and 2‐naphthol polyoxyethylene (NPE), insoluble BA molecules form nanoaggregates with NPE and are stably dispersed within the aqueous electrolyte. At both interfaces, the BA−NPE nanoaggregates form hydrophobic interfacial layers that prevent water attack, thereby effectively suppressing side reactions. In addition, BA−NPE nanoaggregates substantially increase the nucleation overpotential and form a fluorine‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), promoting dendrite‐free Zn plating/stripping. Consequently, the Zn//Zn cell exhibits stable cycling for over 4500 h at 1 mA cm−2 and 1 mAh cm−2. More impressively, the Zn//NH4V4O10 pouch cell delivers capacities exceeding 1.3 Ah for over 900 cycles with a retention rate of 81.8%, validating the significance of the insoluble ligand strategy under practical conditions.

title:
Group Theory-Guided
Orbital Symmetry Engineering of  cis -Quinacridone:
From Symmetry-Forbidden to Dipole-Allowed
Transitions for Efficient Narrowband Emissions
content:
Abstract
Although group theory is widely used to analyze symmetry and electronic transition selection rules in condensed matter physics and coordination chemistry, its use as a predictive design tool for organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) remains largely unexplored. This is particularly important for highly symmetric emitters, where orbital-symmetry constraints can render the lowest-energy transition symmetry-forbidden. Herein, guided by quantum-chemical and group-theoretical analyses, we revisit the long-known cis- and trans-quinacridone isomers and reveal that the lowest-energy transition of cis-quinacridone (cis-QA) is symmetry-forbidden, resulting in a negligible transition dipole moment and intrinsically weak emission. We address this limitation through a group theory-guided orbital-symmetry engineering strategy based on carbonyl-to-imine transformation of the cis-QA skeleton. This targeted structural modification reorganizes the frontier orbital symmetry, converting the lowest-energy transition from symmetry-forbidden to dipole-allowed, while preserving the rigid, highly symmetric molecular framework and suppressing excited-state structural relaxation and vibronic coupling. The resulting cis-I2A2 derivatives exhibit high photoluminescence quantum yields (ΦPL) of 70–99% and narrow emission bandwidths with full-widths at half-maximum (fwhm’s) of 20–32 nm. An OLED based on cis-I2A2-3 delivers narrowband yellow electroluminescence with an emission maximum at 550 nm, a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 32.4%, and substantially mitigated efficiency roll-off relative to conventional cis-quinacridone emitters. This work establishes orbital-symmetry engineering as a rational strategy for decoupling orbital symmetry from overall molecular symmetry, providing a general approach to transforming intrinsically weak luminophores into efficient narrowband emitters.

title:
Divergent Synthesis
of Chiral-at-Sulfur Sulfoximines
via Photoredox/Rhodium-Catalyzed Enantioselective C–H Activation
content:
Abstract
The merger of photoredox catalysis with transition-metal catalysis has emerged as a powerful platform for sustainable synthesis, yet asymmetric variants of photoinduced transition-metal-catalyzed C–H activation remain largely unexplored. Herein, we report a visible-light-driven Rh(III)/chiral carboxylic acid (CCA) cooperative catalytic system that enables the tunable divergent synthesis of two distinct classes of chiral sulfur-containing scaffolds from common sulfoximine and alkyne substrates. Through precise modulation of the reaction conditions, the reaction can be selectively steered toward either the annulation product or the ring-opened product with high enantioselectivities (up to 97% ee). This work provides the first example of asymmetric photoredox/group 9 CpXM(III)-catalyzed C–H functionalization and highlights reactive oxygen species as programmable selectivity switches in asymmetric catalysis.

title:
Resination-Assembled
Soft Multiaxial Molecular Ferroelectrics
Enable Exceptional Low-Electric Field Polarization Switching
content:
Abstract
Resination of soft polymer ferroelectrics has recently emerged as a promising avenue to assemble high- performance electroactive materials, due to the coupling of ferroelectricity with enhanced mechanical and processable merits. However, it remains a huge challenge to stabilize ferroelectricity and dipolar activity at the resin–ferroelectric interface. For the first time, we adopt here the resination assembling strategy into the soft molecule-based ferroelectric (BZA)2(DMA)BiI6 (1, BZA = benzylammonium; DMA = dimethylammonium), which enables the unusual ferroelectric behavior of low-electric field switching of polarization. Compound 1 is a high-temperature multiaxial ferroelectric with six possible equivalent polarization directions and a low coercive electric field, arising from its stepwise phase transitions around 350 K (Tc). Strikingly, the precise resination of 1 with the epoxy-matrix composite yields a highly loaded composite with a microscopic cross-linked structure, whose polarization can be switched under a quite low coercive electric field (Ec ∼ 3.8 kV/cm). These shape-customized ferroelectric resin wafers of 1 have superior antielectric fatigue attributes after ∼104 cycles. Moreover, these wafers exhibit enhanced resistance to localized deformation, evidenced by a 30.9% decrease in maximum penetration depth relative to the bulk single crystals. As the first study on the resination of molecular ferroelectrics, our findings bridge the gap between molecular ferroelectrics and material engineering, which highlights the application potential of resinated molecular ferroelectrics.

title:
Macrocycle Screening
against the C-Terminal
Region of CHD4 Uncovers Its Role as an Interaction Hub in the Formation
of the Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase Complex
content:
Abstract
The Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase complex (NuRD) plays a key role in regulating hemoglobin expression in adult erythroid cells. Selectively disrupting this complex potently induces the expression of fetal hemoglobin, a proven therapeutic strategy for treating beta-hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell anemia. In these studies, we have used mRNA display to identify small macrocyclic peptides that inhibit the interaction between two core components of NuRD, the SANT-SLIDE domain of CHD4 and the CR2 domain of GATAD2A. In addition, the screen suggested a second binding site on the CHD4 domain. Based on this observation, we hypothesized and confirmed that CDK2AP1 bound to this region of CHD4, leading us to purify and determine the structure of the ternary complex between CHD4, GATAD2A, and CDK2AP1. The results of our studies show that the SANT-SLIDE domain of CHD4 functions as a critical interaction hub in the formation of NuRD and suggest a strategy to block NuRD function for therapy.

title:
Linkage-Engineered
Fabrication of a Robust 1,6-Anthrazoline-Linked
Covalent Organic Framework with Significantly Promoted Exciton Dissociation
for Superior Photocatalysis
content:
Abstract
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are promising polymeric photocatalysts for solar-driven hydrogen evolution, yet their performance is often hampered by tightly bound excitons that suppress efficient charge separation. Herein, we present a linkage engineering strategy that directly attenuates excitonic effects through a facile two-step postsynthetic protocol combining imine bond locking with site-specific protonation. This approach affords a new class of readily functionalizable 1,6-anthrazoline-linked COFs (TP-PACOFs) featuring cationic, fully conjugated backbones with high planarity, tunable donor–acceptor character, and well-preserved crystallinity. Such a structurally synergistic design enables the cyano-containing derivative, TP-PACOF-CN, to overcome the “trade-off” barrier among synthetic accessibility, light-harvesting capability, exciton binding strength, surface wettability, and chemical stability. Strikingly, TP-PACOF-CN achieves a benchmark sacrificial photocatalytic hydrogen evolution rate of 307.8 mmol g–1 h–1 under visible-light irradiation, which is 1.9 times higher than that of its biquinoline-linked analogue and surpasses nearly all reported COF-based photocatalysts. Moreover, it delivers an apparent quantum yield (AQY) of 31.6% at 420 nm, retains activity up to 700 nm (AQY = 1.9%) and exhibits excellent recyclability. Comprehensive spectroscopic investigations and theoretical simulations demonstrate that the ingenious architectural motif of TP-PACOF-CN significantly promotes exciton dissociation and facilitates charge-carrier dynamics. This work provides valuable insights into exciton management in organic semiconductors and underscores the potential of structurally engineered COFs for high-efficiency solar fuel production.

title:
Artificial
Light-Harvesting Nanotubes: Intermolecular
Charge Transfer beyond the Exciton Model
content:
Abstract
Self-assembled nanotubes of C8S3 cyanine dyes have been widely investigated as model systems for light-harvesting complexes. Recently published data point to a brick-layer molecular arrangement in the nanotubes, in contrast to the herringbone structure previously adopted to explain the absorption and linear dichroism data within the exciton model. Here we solve this conundrum by showing that, relying on the brick-layer structure as extracted from cryo-EM, the exciton model can properly account for the observed spectral features, provided it is extended to account for intermolecular charge-transfer interactions.

title:
Integrated Solid/Solution
NMR Assignment Enables Mapping
of Dynamics and Ligand Binding in a 134 kDa Enzyme
content:
Abstract
Understanding enzyme function requires characterizing not only the static structure but also dynamics and ligand interactions. NMR spectroscopy provides this insight at atomic resolution, yet for large proteins, the difficulty of resonance assignment has largely confined such studies to systems below ∼50 kDa, or to observing only methyl groups. Here, we present an integrated magic-angle spinning (MAS) and solution NMR study of the 134 kDa tetrameric malate dehydrogenase from Ignicoccus islandicus (IiMDH), an enzyme of particular interest as an evolutionary intermediate between allosteric lactate dehydrogenases and nonallosteric malate dehydrogenases. By combining high-dimensional (up to 4D) MAS NMR experiments on sedimented protein with solution NMR, we achieved 92% backbone heavy-atom assignment and 91% assignment of all Ile-δ1, Leu-δ1/-δ2, Val-γ1/-γ2, Met-ε, and Thr-γ methyl groups. Building on these assignments, we used various probes of backbone and side-chain dynamics: elevated MAS NMR 15N rotating-frame relaxation (R1ρ) points to slow motions in functionally critical regions, including the catalytic loop and the mobile surface loop. Complementary methyl-axis order parameters from solution NMR identified additional flexible sites in the hydrophobic core. Chemical shift perturbation experiments upon addition of the substrate analogue oxamate, monitored via backbone 1H–15N TROSY, revealed both active-site contacts and responses in helices α2F and α3G, regions associated with signal transmission in allosteric homologues. The integrated approach demonstrated here exploits the distinct strengths of MAS and solution NMR and provides a comprehensive view of structure, dynamics, and substrate interactions in a large oligomeric enzyme that neither technique could provide alone.

title:
Probing the Conformational
Behavior of a Seven Hetero-Spin
Supramolecule
content:
Abstract
The synthesis and crystal structure of a 7-spin supramolecular poly-rotaxane is reported. The [4]rotaxane structure involves a trigonal thread centred on a {CrNi2} core, with each of the three arms terminated by Cu(II) centres and bearing a {Cr7Ni} metallocycle. The macromolecule brings together three distinct electron spin centers. Continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy confirms the molecule remains intact in solution, with the three types of spin center each uniquely addressable. Orientation-selective Double Electron Electron Resonance (DEER) and Relaxation Induced Dipolar Modulation Enhancement (RIDME) spectroscopies are used to selectively probe the different spin-spin interactions in the frozen solution phase and to define differences from the solid-state crystal structure.

title:
Encapsulation-Activated
Deep-NIR Triarylmethane Dyes
via Steric Hindrance Engineering for Long-Circulating Fluorescence/Photoacoustic
Dual-Modal Bioimaging
content:
Abstract
NIR-II fluorescence/photoacoustic dual-modal imaging offers complementary advantages in sensitivity and penetration depth. However, its efficacy is compromised by aggregation, nonspecific binding, and background interference, which persist even with polymeric encapsulation. To address these limitations, we report herein the rationally designed encapsulation-activated triarylmethane dyes (ED5) functionalized with bulky 1,8-bis(2,4,6-trimethylphenoxy)anthracene (1,8-BMPhA) moieties. The judiciously installed bulky substituents not only impart sufficient steric hindrance to repel protein binding and suppress intermolecular π–π stacking but also favor a locally near-coplanar geometry of the conjugated backbone, thereby preserving a high oscillator strength and a large molar extinction coefficient. Upon DSPE-PEG2000 encapsulation, nanoconfinement restricts intramolecular rotation and suppresses nonradiative decay, triggering a marked turn-on response of both fluorescence and photoacoustic signals. The optimized ED5_3@NPs exhibit a 14-fold fluorescence enhancement, a molar extinction coefficient of 71,000 M–1 cm–1, and a photothermal conversion efficiency of 62%. In vivo, they enable sustained high-quality imaging over a 51-h period, achieve crosstalk-free vascular-lymphatic dual-channel visualization, and afford high-contrast orthotopic liver tumor diagnosis against strong background interference. This encapsulation-activated strategy overcomes the long-standing constraints of NIR-II fluorophores, including low molar extinction coefficient, aggregation propensity, poor water solubility, and low photothermal conversion efficiency. It offers a general and well-defined paradigm for high-fidelity deep-tissue imaging and provides a promising strategy for further development of precision diagnostics.

title:
Migratory Hydroamination
of Alkenes via Iron-Hydride
Catalysis
content:
Abstract
The renaissance of catalytic metal hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) offers advanced tools for hydroamination of alkenes. Despite these merits, state-of-the-art MHAT hydroamination protocols are largely limited to intermolecular coupling or intramolecular cyclization, thereby necessitating new catalytic platforms to explore MHAT reactivity and access unexplored hydroamination reaction pathways. Herein, we report an iron hydride-catalyzed migratory hydroamination of allylamines, enabled by a sequential MHAT process with finely tuned 1,2-amino migration. This strategy converts readily accessible allylamines into structurally diverse alkylamines and β-amino acids through a three-step radical cascade. This protocol features a broad tolerance toward a range of functional groups, encompassing complex drug and natural product derivatives. Beyond providing an efficient approach to medicinally relevant amine scaffolds, this work establishes a new paradigm for MHAT-enabled molecular editing through radical functional group migration, thereby expanding the synthetic repertoire of alkene hydroamination.

title:
Coordination-Site
Engineering Enables Synergistic
π-Coupling in Peroxomolybdates
content:
Abstract
Achieving constructive coupling among multiple second-harmonic-generation (SHG)-active units remains a major challenge in the development of high-performance nonlinear optical (NLO) crystals. Herein, we introduce a coordination-site occupation strategy that enables precise regulation of the geometric arrangement and electronic coupling among three SHG-active components: a delocalized π-conjugated organic ligand, a d0 Mo6+ center, and a localized π-conjugated peroxide ligand. Application of this strategy to a peroxomolybdate system affords three new complexes with progressively increasing coordination-site occupancy. The optimized compound, [MoO(O2)(H2O)(C7H3NO4)] (III), crystallizes in a noncentrosymmetric structure and exhibits a record powder SHG response of 34.9 × KH2PO4 at 1300 nm, together with phase-matching behavior and an impressive laser-induced damage threshold of 5.8 GW/cm2, representing the highest SHG performance reported to date for a peroxomolybdate complex. Computational analyses reveal that the nearly parallel alignment between the organic π-conjugated plane and the Mo–peroxide plane maximizes electronic coupling and hyperpolarizability, thereby giving rise to the exceptional second-order NLO performance. These findings establish coordination-site occupation as a general crystal-engineering strategy for synergistically integrating multiple SHG-active units and provide a rational framework for the design of next-generation high-performance nonlinear optical materials.

title:
Bioinspired Quantum-Guided
Engineering of Activatable
Probes via Intermolecular Electron Transfer for Single-Cell Molecular
Diagnosis
content:
Abstract
Fluorescence imaging holds theoretical sensitivity for single-cell molecular diagnosis, yet practical performance is limited by residual probe-intrinsic fluorescence arising from incomplete control of intramolecular electron transfer within the probe scaffold. Inspired by natural photosynthesis, where spatially organized pigments enable quantum-coherent excitation transport and precise intermolecular electron transfer, we develop a bioinspired quantum chemistry-guided engineering (BQCE) strategy that programs intermolecular electron transfer to construct molecular assembly based background-eliminating activatable molecule probes (BEAMs). Guided by BQCE, the peroxynitrite-responsive hemicyanine-based BEAM1, despite the intrinsically difficult-to-quench nature of this fluorophore scaffold, achieves near-zero background fluorescence, 103.5-fold activation, and an unprecedented detection limit of 1.3 nM. BEAM1 resolves basal ONOO– fluxes at single-cell resolution, enabling single-cell molecular diagnosis that distinguishes malignant from normal cells based solely on endogenous redox signatures. In vivo, BEAM1 enables detection of lymph nodes containing sparsely distributed metastatic cells, with subsequent ex vivo histological analysis identifying metastatic deposits as small as ∼ 35 μm, extending fluorescence imaging into the regime of single-cell level early cancer detection.

title:
π-Armor:
Shape-Complementary Encapsulation
of Aromatics
content:
Abstract
Host–guest binding can be classified into two well-separated modes, i.e., reversible binding under thermodynamic control and permanent encapsulation via kinetic trapping during host formation. However, combining both modes within a single π-conjugated host on the basis of host–guest shape complementarity has remained challenging. Here, we present the design and synthesis of a neutral D3-symmetric π-conjugated cage (1), wherein two curved hexa-cata-hexabenzocoronene (c-HBC) panels are bridged by dibenzodiazocine (DBDA) units to form three orifices and a biconvex nanocavity. Cage 1 reversibly encapsulates aromatic guests, whereby binding affinities are governed by dispersion arising from shape complementarity. In contrast, bulky guests that are too large to pass through the orifices are incorporated during cage formation and permanently entrapped, affording thermally robust carceplexes. Even a π-extended guest exceeding the cavity size was entrapped, with its aryl groups protruding through the three orifices to form a mechanically interlocked molecule. Thus, cage 1 behaves as a dual-mode host controlled by shape complementarity, representing a “π-armor” that sandwiches aromatic guests between its π-surfaces.

title:
Entropy-Driven Dynamic
Oxygen Cycling on High-Entropy
Oxides Enables Coke-Resistant Dry Reforming of Methane
content:
Abstract
Catalyst deactivation caused by carbon deposition and metal sintering remains a major challenge for dry reforming of methane (DRM). Herein, we designed and synthesized a Ce-based high-entropy oxide catalyst (NiCoMgAlZrCe-HEO). Configurational entropy stabilizes a multication-disordered lattice with pronounced local distortion, which modulates the oxygen coordination environment and enhances the lattice-oxygen reactivity. The NiCo alloy nanoparticles formed through in situ reductive exsolution are anchored to the HEO matrix, thereby enhancing the resistance to sintering. The reduced NiCoMgAlZrCe-HEO exhibits CH4 and CO2 conversions of 80.2% and 87.3%, respectively, at 700 °C and maintains stable catalytic performance over 500 h. Combined experimental characterization and density functional theory calculations reveal a dynamic oxygen-cycling mechanism enabled by the high-entropy structure. Mobile lattice oxygen favors the selective activation of CH4 by promoting the formation of *CH3O intermediates, thereby suppressing the carbon-forming pathways. Meanwhile, abundant oxygen vacancies facilitate CO2 activation, accelerating the replenishment of the reactive lattice oxygen. This work offers a feasible strategy for designing DRM catalysts that are resistant to coking and sintering based on configurational entropy regulation.

title:
Indenyl-Benzyl Radical
Recombination Leads to the
Formation of Fluoranthene, a Non-Alternant Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon
content:
Abstract
Nonalternant polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) incorporating five-membered rings are fundamental intermediates linking planar aromatics to curved carbon nanostructures including fullerenes and nanotubes, yet their formation mechanisms are not fully understood. The detection of fluoranthene (C16H10) in samples from the near-Earth carbonaceous asteroid 162,173 Ryugu and 101,955 Bennu highlights the need for chemically viable pathways under both combustion and astrochemical conditions. Here, we demonstrate that fluoranthene forms efficiently commencing with barrierless recombination of resonance-stabilized indenyl (C9H7•) and benzyl (C7H7•) radicals. Microreactor experiments combined with electronic structure calculations reveal rapid carbon–carbon bond formation, cyclization, and dehydrogenation to the nonalternant framework. This mechanism represents an alternative to stepwise acetylene addition and enables early incorporation of pentagonal motifs during molecular growth. These findings establish radical–radical recombination as a versatile route to nonalternant PAHs, providing a unified framework for their formation in high-temperature combustion systems and carbon-rich astrophysical environments like circumstellar envelopes of carbon stars and planetary nebulae as their descendants.

title:
Substrate Length Controls
Atropopeptide Complexity
and Triggers Excision-Driven Scaffold Hop to Diketopiperazine Alkaloids
content:
Abstract
Atropopeptides are a family of ribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally modified peptides (RiPPs) that share conserved cross-link-forming amino acids in their core peptides, yet adopt architectures ranging from simple monocyclic to complex polycyclic structures with intriguing three-dimensional shapes. These complex architectures arise from multiple C–C and C–N cross-links that are installed by a single cytochrome P450 enzyme, but the factors governing these divergent cross-linking patterns and resulting structural complexities have remained elusive. Recent studies on RiPP biosynthesis have revealed a form of substrate-controlled catalysis, in which the precursor sequence, rather than the modifying enzyme, dictates the reaction course. Here, we describe a distinct form of substrate-controlled catalysis in atropopeptide biosynthesis, demonstrating that core peptide length, rather than sequence, determines the cross-linking pattern installed by an atropopeptide-forming cytochrome P450. We further uncover an unusual proteolytic excision of an internal amino acid in mature atropopeptides, generating peptides that spontaneously convert into pyrroloindoline-containing diketopiperazines (DKPs) and thereby effecting a nonenzymatic scaffold-hop from atropopeptides to DKP-derived alkaloids, for which we provide mechanistic insight. Both the atropopeptide and the corresponding DKP exhibit antiviral activity, and their structural diversity can be further expanded through precursor engineering. Our work reveals substrate length as a key determinant of atropopeptide complexity, provides insights into the catalysis of a multicross-link-forming P450, and establishes an unprecedented route connecting atropopeptides to pyrroloindoline DKP alkaloids.

title: Electrochemical energy conversion beyond Earth
content: Terrestrial electrochemical design implicitly relies on Earth-bound physics, such as gravity and natural convection. Beyond Earth, where these conditions no longer apply, we argue that designing with architecture, co-integrating electrochemical, thermal, and mechanical functions into a single structure, emerges as a primary physical variable rather than a downstream choice. Furthermore, additive manufacturing enables rapid structural iteration, allowing electrochemical energy conversion devices to be tailored to the strict operational demands of both space environments and resource-limited terrestrial applications.

title:
Multiscale
Simulation on Using Phase Change Materials
to Mitigate Natural Gas Hydrate Dissociation during Deep-Sea Well
Cementing
content:
Abstract
In deep-sea natural gas hydrates (NGHs) exploitation, heat released during well cementing can cause hydrate dissociation and natural gas release into the cement slurry, potentially triggering major engineering accidents such as wellbore collapse and environmental hazards. Although microencapsulated phase change materials (MPCMs) have been widely used for thermal regulation in cementitious composites, their potential to mitigate temperature rise in realistic deep-sea well-cementing conditions remains underinvestigated. To examine the influence of MPCM-cement composites on the thermal stability of NGHs, this study develops a multiscale simulation framework that integrates equivalent medium theory, cement hydration kinetics, and PCM properties to analyze transient heat transfer between MPCM-cement composites and the NGH-bearing surrounding. An equivalent surface heat source derived from small-scale simulations enables efficient reservoir-scale thermal modeling without the need to resolve complex wellbore components. The proposed model, validated against experimental and field data, indicates that cement hydration can induce a hydrate-dissociation zone up to 15.3 m, whereas using only 5% MPCMs by volume for well cementing reduces this thickness by up to 81.7%. Key engineering parameters, including geothermal gradient, seawater depth, well geometry, and PCM properties, are systematically quantified to provide practical guidance for thermal management during deep-sea NGH well cementing.

title:
Mesopore-Engineered
Zeolite Boosts Depolymerization
of Technical Lignin
content:
Abstract
The cleavage of recalcitrant methylene linkages in technical lignin is critical for its valorization but remains inefficient due to poor mass transfer in microporous catalysts. Here, we report a simple alkaline desilication treatment of commercial Hβ zeolite that creates open mesopores without compromising acidity. The resulting hierarchical catalyst enhances oligomer diffusion, boosting the yield of monomeric and dimeric phenolics from the depolymerization of five technical lignin oligomers to 9.8–25.2 wt %, which is a 1.9- to 2.7-fold increase relative to conventional hydrogenolysis that only cleaves C–O bonds. Complete hydrodeoxygenation of these phenolics yields a mixture of mono- and bicyclic cycloalkanes with a carbon-number (C9–C20) distribution overlapping that of Jet-A fuel, highlighting their potential as drop-in blending components for sustainable aviation fuel. This work provides a scalable, cost-effective, and green catalytic route that directly addresses the mass-transfer bottleneck in technical lignin depolymerization.

title:
Synthesis
and Dissociation of Gas Hydrate with Added
Biosurfactants
content:
Abstract
Microorganisms located in the hydrate pores produce biosurfactants that reduce the surface tension of water. However, the effect of biosurfactants on the characteristics of hydrate synthesis and dissociation is understudied, although it could significantly improve the efficiency of gas extraction from hydrates. In this study, the kinetics of methane hydrate formation and dissociation was investigated in the presence of three biosurfactants. Three regasification stages were identified. It was found that adding 0.5 vol % Surfactin, C5H12N2O2, or C2H7NO3S to an aqueous solution reduces the methane hydrate synthesis time by 21, 13.7, and 11%, respectively. Adding 10 vol % sand to an aqueous solution of Surfactin reduced the hydrate synthesis time by 24%, but the gas saturation was 6–10% less than that when using other additives. During the dissociation of methane hydrate with Surfactin, the rate of this process increased by 12–62% compared to hydrates with C5H12N2O2 and C2H7NO3S. Based on the obtained results, equations were derived to predict the hydrate dissociation time as a function of its heating intensity. Finally, a conceptual technology was proposed for the environmentally friendly heat generation using gas hydrates on the basis of the research findings.

title:
Enhancing
Hydrate Exploitation from Reservoirs by
Depressurization Combined with Electrical Resistance Heating
content:
Abstract
Natural gas hydrate (NGH) production by depressurization can be constrained by the temperature decline associated with endothermic hydrate dissociation and the resulting potential for secondary hydrate formation. To address these limitations, this study investigates electrical resistance heating (ERH), which generates Joule heat within hydrate-bearing sediments. A laboratory-scale electrical–thermal–hydraulic–chemical (ETHC) coupled model is developed, incorporating Joule heating, multiphase flow, heat transfer, and hydrate dissociation kinetics. Following validation against the Masuda core experiment, three production scenarios are compared: depressurization alone (Case A), depressurization combined with ERH (Case B), and depressurization combined with ERH and external thermal replenishment (Case C). Under a constant external boundary temperature of 273.15 K, gas production in Case A declines rapidly as dissociation-induced cooling inhibits further hydrate dissociation. ERH in Case B promotes dissociation within the core, although the same boundary temperature continues to constrain dissociation near the periphery. In Case C, raising the external boundary temperature to 280.15 K alleviates this constraint and promotes more spatially extensive hydrate dissociation. Compared with Case B, Case C increases the peak gas production rate by 64% and accelerates the dissociation process. These results clarify the combined effects of internal Joule heating and external thermal replenishment on hydrate dissociation under idealized laboratory-scale thermal boundary conditions.

title:
Joule-Heated
Woven Fiber Contactors for Direct Air
Capture
content:
Abstract
Practical direct air capture (DAC) demands a sorbent contactor that simultaneously delivers high active-material loading, low flow resistance, efficient mass transfer, and rapid regeneration─requirements that conventional sorbent architectures rarely satisfy together. Here, we present a woven fiber contactor that addresses these requirements by interlacing dry-fabricated zeolite Y/PTFE fibers with copper wire supports into a structured contactor. Compared to a stacked laminate configuration, the woven sorbent exhibited markedly more efficient mass transfer, yielding a narrower mass transfer zone (LMTZ = 4.4 mm and 11.1 mm at 50 sccm) and a steeper breakthrough front. This structural advantage translated into robust sorption performance, with CO2 capture capacity varying by only 11.7% across a 10-fold increase in feed flow rate (50–500 sccm, corresponding to superficial velocities 5.79 × 10–3 to 5.79 × 10–2 m/s) compared to 19.2% for the stacked laminate. The woven architecture further reduced pressure drop by 7- to 18-fold over a wide range of superficial velocities (1.16 × 10–2–5.79 × 10–1 m/s). The integrated copper wires enabled electrified temperature swing adsorption (e-TSA) with near-instantaneous heating, driving CO2 desorption within 1 min. Over 10 consecutive adsorption–desorption cycles, the module retained an average capacity of 1.01 mmol/gsorbent with less than 6.93% variance. Together, these results establish the woven fiber contactor as a scalable platform that unites high sorbent loading, low flow resistance, efficient mass transfer, and rapid electrified regeneration for energy-efficient DAC.

title:
Temperature
and Pressure Effects on CO 2  Foam Aging Revealed by Multi-Descriptor
Optical Analysis and Complementary
High-Pressure Evaluation
content:
Abstract
Optical methods are widely used to evaluate foam stability, but their signals integrate liquid drainage, phase redistribution, bubble-size evolution, and coalescence, limiting mechanism-specific interpretation. This study applies a measurement-aware, multidescriptor strategy combining bench-scale Turbiscan screening, an independent high-pressure CO2-foam visual-cell campaign, and porous-media core-flood evaluation. At 30, 45, and 60 °C, initial gas entrainment, liquid drainage, apparent optical bubble evolution, foam–liquid boundary migration, regional backscattering variation, and the Turbiscan Stability Index were evaluated. High-pressure CO2-foam performance was independently assessed over 12–22 MPa using maximum foam volume and foam half-life. Increasing temperature enhanced initial gas entrainment but accelerated subsequent structural aging, as indicated by faster drainage, earlier boundary migration, a higher apparent cubic-radius evolution coefficient, and greater cumulative optical variation. The apparent cubic-radius evolution coefficient increased from 1.14 × 105 to 2.27 × 105 μm3·min–1 between 30 and 60 °C. In the high-pressure campaign, increasing target pressure under the adopted density-based charging protocol was associated with higher maximum foam volume and longer half-life, although the adverse effect of elevated temperature remained. Because CO2 inventory, surfactant-stock charge, and ethanol content covaried with target-state CO2 density, this trend is interpreted as a combined pressure–charge/formulation response rather than an isolated thermodynamic pressure effect. At 22 MPa, increasing temperature from 30 to 60 °C reduced the maximum foam volume from approximately 1190 to 865 mL and the half-life from 198 to 125 min. The core-flood experiments provided initial porous-media evidence: CO2/E-1340 foam increased the final oil recovery factor to 53.24%, compared with 40.79% for CO2 flooding and 26.97% for brine flooding. During foam treatment, the differential pressure increased from 0.26 to 2.68 MPa and stabilized at 1.98 MPa after treatment, corresponding to a resistance factor of 10.308 and a residual resistance factor of 7.615. These results extend the bulk-cell and high-pressure screening observations to initial porous-media evidence of increased flow resistance and improved displacement performance under the tested conditions. Broader validation using additional reservoir-fluid systems and multiple core conditions, together with experiments that independently decouple pressure from CO2 inventory, remains necessary before the results can be generalized to formation-specific EOR or CCUS applications.

title: Facet-Dependent Plating/Stripping Behavior and Crystallographic Evolution during Cycling on Zn Metal Anodes
content:
Abstract
Aqueous zinc metal batteries offer a safe and low-cost option for scalable energy storage; however, their practical reversibility is limited by nonuniform Zn plating/stripping and dendritic growth. Here, Zn single-crystal electrodes exposing well-defined (002), (100), and (101) crystalline facets were used to isolate the role of crystallography in Zn metal cycling. Zn deposition is strongly facet-dependent, forming hexagonal, rectangular/prismatic, and corner-defined morphologies on (002), (100), and (101) facets, respectively. Time-dependent SEM further reveals that Zn growth proceeds via discrete edge- or corner-initiated crystallographic units rather than uniform terrace coverage. During stripping, Zn metal is removed via facet-preserved mesoscopic dissolution domains, leaving geometry-defined pits rather than random corrosion-like features. However, these pits are not preferentially refilled during subsequent plating. Repeated cycling redirects Zn growth to protrusions and roughened regions, causing mossy/dendritic accumulation, mixed-texture evolution, and loss of epitaxial reversibility. These findings highlight the need to control both oriented deposition and poststripping surface reconstruction.

title: Self-Healing Armor Enables Electrode Integrity and Interfacial Stability for Durable Silicon Anodes
content:
Abstract
Polymer coatings are widely used to stabilize silicon anodes, yet repeated volume changes can fracture the coating and accelerate continuous SEI reconstruction. Here, we construct a self-healing fluorinated acrylate/methacrylate copolymer coating in situ on silicon-based anodes through the UV-induced copolymerization of HFBA and MPS. The resulting copolymer combines strong adhesion with dynamic self-recovery through reversible dipole-dipole interactions, enabling microcrack repair within 1 min. Meanwhile, the HFBA-derived segments act as a fluorine reservoir, promoting the formation of a thin SEI with a polymer-rich outer layer and a LiF-rich inner layer. Consequently, SiOx-P(HFBA+MPS)||Li cells deliver 73.5% capacity retention after 500 cycles at 800 mA g–1. A practical 1.5 Ah NCM811||Si/C/Gr-P(HFBA+MPS) pouch cell achieves 71.9% capacity retention after 300 cycles and shows improved thermal safety. This work provides a scalable strategy for durable and safe silicon-based batteries by integrating autonomous self-healing of the polymer coating with sustained fluorine-assisted interphase stabilization.

title: Lightweight CNT Fabric Current Collectors Enabling Silicon Anodes in High-Capacity Lithium-Ion Batteries
content:
Abstract
Conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) require metallic current collectors such as copper for anodes and aluminum for cathodes, adding significant weight without contributing to the capacity. This is especially problematic for Si-dominant anodes, with mass loadings lower than 2 mg cm–2. Here, copper is replaced with lightweight, non-woven carbon nanotube fabrics (CNTfs) combined with high-capacity Si/PPAN active material to form a self-standing composite anode. This lightweight electrode delivers a capacity of 1000 mAh g–1 (normalized with respect to the total Si/PPAN/CNTf anode weight) for over 700 cycles at a current density of 1 A g–1 and can potentially boost the cell-level energy density by ∼25% when paired with commercial cathodes. Cross-sectional SEM-EDX imaging and peel tests confirm excellent interfacial contact between the Si/PPAN layer and CNTf current collector. Furthermore, the effects of increasing CNTf thickness reveal more evident SEI formation in the CNTf layer, lowering the first-cycle Coulombic efficiency. These findings demonstrate the potential of using CNTfs in high-energy LIBs, while also reducing emissions associated with metal manufacturing.

title: Development of Na-Containing Ce–Mn Composite Redox Materials for Integrated Thermochemical Energy Storage and Air Separation Process
content:
Abstract
This study proposes an integrated thermochemical energy storage and air separation process and investigates Na-containing Ce–Mn composite oxides as candidate redox materials. The materials were prepared by coprecipitation, and the effects of coprecipitation temperature and Ce mixing ratio on their redox characteristics were evaluated under temperature-swing conditions involving reduction at 550 °C and oxidation at 350 °C. The largest redox swing of 2.5 wt % was obtained at a coprecipitation temperature of 5 °C and a Ce mixing ratio of 7.5 mol %. XRD analysis confirmed the formation of Na0.7MnO2, whose presence was correlated with higher redox performance. The heat of reaction per unit oxygen exchange remained largely constant regardless of Ce loading, suggesting that Ce incorporation did not predominantly contribute as a direct oxygen storage mechanism under the investigated conditions and that Mn-based redox reactions constituted the dominant contribution to oxygen exchange. Repeated redox cycling showed a gradual decrease in redox swing, although reversible oxygen exchange was maintained throughout the investigated cycles.

title: Janus-Structured Carbon-Based Water-Evaporation-Induced Generator for Efficient Blue Energy Harvesting and Marine Cathodic Protection
content:
Abstract
Water-evaporation-induced energy harvesting has emerged as a promising blue energy technology; however, widespread application is hindered by water-saturation-induced instability and limited functionality. Herein, a low-cost flexible Janus water-evaporation-induced generator (WIG) is fabricated via facile immersion and spray-coating methods. Ketjen carbon black with a high specific surface area (1196.76 m2/g) serves as a conductive filler, while the PVDF-modified asymmetric structure effectively suppresses overhydration and maintains a durable wet-dry gradient. After systematic optimization, the device achieves maximum outputs of 1.0 V and 557 μA in a 12 wt % NaCl solution, delivering a cumulative energy density of 1100.3 kJ m–2 L–1 and 267.23 J m–2 in deionized water and seawater, respectively. Assembled modules enable capacitor charging and the operation of low-power electronics. Furthermore, a self-powered cathodic protection system is established to sustain a current density of 400 μA cm–2 for 12 h, enabling efficient marine corrosion protection. This work demonstrates a scalable dual-functional WIG, providing valuable insights into the development of advanced multifunctional blue energy devices.

title: Surface Fluorination of LiNi 0.5 Mn 1.5 O 4  by Fluoropolymer Thermal Decomposition: From Reactive Gas Speciation to Electrochemical Stabilization
content:
Abstract
Surface fluorination is an effective strategy to stabilize high-voltage LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 (LNMO) cathodes against interfacial degradation, yet the role of the fluorinating agent and its decomposition pathway in governing surface speciation remains poorly understood. Here, PTFE and CYTOP are investigated as solid fluoropolymer-derived fluorinating agents for LNMO surface modification via thermal decomposition under inert atmosphere, yielding comparable surface fluorine contents of approximately 0.08 mmol g–1 for both treatments. X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy confirm that both treatments preserve the cubic spinel framework, indicating that fluorination is confined to the particle surface. XPS reveals the formation of LiF-like species, M–F bonds and manganese oxyfluoride-like environments, while EPR reveals modifications of the manganese electronic environment after treatment. Galvanostatic cycling over 100 cycles at C/10 demonstrates improved capacity retention for both fluorinated samples: all three electrodes deliver an initial discharge capacity close to 143 mAh g–1. After 100 cycles, LNMO–PTFE retains 95% of its initial discharge capacity (136 mAh g–1), compared to 91% for LNMO–CYTOP and 90% for pristine LNMO (∼128 mAh g–1). TGA-MS and in situ gas-phase FTIR identify the reactive species generated during decomposition: PTFE mainly releases :CF2, •CF, •C2F3 and •CF3 fragments, whereas CYTOP produces a broader distribution of fluorinated species over a wider temperature range. These differences in decomposition chemistry directly control the nature of the fluorinated interphase and the resulting electrochemical stabilization of LNMO. This work establishes mechanistic guidelines for designing scalable fluoropolymer-based surface treatments for high-voltage cathode materials, as an alternative to reactive fluorine sources such as F2 or XeF2.

title: Post‐Processing Strategies for Laser‐Scribed Grooves in Perovskite Solar Modules: Mechanisms, Trade‐Offs, and Engineering Guidelines
content:
This work systematically accounts for the damage cascade mechanisms associated with laser‐scribed grooves in perovskite solar modules, classifies and evaluates posttreatment strategies and their technical trade‐offs, and establishes engineering design principles for industrial implementation, offering theoretical and process‐level guidance for developing efficient and stable large‐area modules.








ABSTRACT
Monolithic integration is widely regarded as a practical pathway toward scalable perovskite solar modules (PSMs). Despite substantial progress in understanding and mitigating laser‐scribing‐induced damage, laser‐scribed groove regions remain important localized sources of performance loss and degradation that can affect module efficiency, reproducibility, and long‐term stability. While a growing number of studies have reported various post‐processing approaches for laser‐scribed grooves, the field still lacks an engineering‐oriented framework connecting laser‐induced damage mechanisms with practical module‐level mitigation strategies. In this review, we specifically focus on laser‐scribed grooves as functionally dominant degradation zones, rather than treating them as minor processing defects. We introduce an engineering‐oriented damage cascade framework to describe how laser‐induced thermal disorder, defect generation, structural disruption, and transport processes are hierarchically coupled. Based on this perspective, existing post‐processing strategies for grooves are systematically classified according to the stages of the damage cascade they primarily address. This enables a mechanism‐guided evaluation of their effectiveness, trade‐offs, and scalability.

title:
Tuning Second-Sphere
Amine Basicity to Modulate Hydride
Intermediates and Selectivity in Molecular Manganese Bipyridine CO 2  Electroreduction
content:
Abstract
Manganese bipyridine tricarbonyl complexes represent a prominent class of molecular electrocatalysts for efficient and selective CO2-to-CO conversion. Recent efforts have sought to redirect product selectivity toward HCOOH by incorporating second-sphere amine proton relays. However, how the physicochemical properties of second-sphere amines govern catalytic activity and selectivity remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we report a new manganese bipyridine complex bearing 2-(pyrrolidin-1-ylmethyl)phenyl substituents at the 6,6′-positions and systematically evaluate its performance against the diethylamine- and morpholine-functionalized analogs to elucidate the role of second-sphere amine basicity on CO2 reduction. The pyrrolidine-functionalized catalyst achieves near-unity selectivity for HCOOH in acetonitrile with a Faradaic efficiency of 92%, outperforming the corresponding diethylamine (71%) and morpholine (23%) derivatives. This complex also displays outstanding catalytic activity with maximum turnover frequencies of 2300 s–1 and up to 70,000 s–1 under low- and high-overpotential conditions, respectively, ranking among the most active manganese bipyridine catalysts for CO2-to-HCOOH conversion. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the pyrrolidine groups function as proton relays, facilitating proton transfer to the manganese center and promoting formation of the key Mn-hydride intermediate for CO2-to-HCOOH conversion. Density functional theory calculations further demonstrate that the stronger basicity of the pyrrolidine functionality lowers the energy barriers for amine protonation and subsequent intramolecular proton transfer by 3–6 kcal mol–1 relative to the less basic diethylamine and morpholine analogs. Overall, this work establishes second-sphere amine basicity as a key molecular parameter for tuning both activity and product selectivity in the development of molecular CO2 reduction catalysts.

title:
A Standalone Flavoprotein
Monooxygenase Directs Divergent
Tropolone Skeletal Editing through Baeyer–Villiger-Triggered
Rearrangement
content:
Abstract
Late-stage oxidative remodeling of tropolone cores underpins the remarkable scaffold diversity in fungal meroterpenoid biosynthesis. However, the mechanistic basis by which a single enzymatic catalyst diverts a common substrate toward carbon-excising ring contraction versus carbon-retentive skeletal rearrangement remains elusive. Here, via comparative transcriptomics and targeted gene deletion, we identified a standalone host-encoded class A flavoprotein monooxygenase, ANIA_01821 (AN1821), as indispensable for tropolone ring remodeling in Aspergillus nidulans. A functionally homologous enzyme, AO090103000276 (AO276), from Aspergillus oryzae was further characterized as a tractable biocatalyst for in vitro studies. Reconstitution assays using purified AO276 revealed that this single flavoprotein monooxygenase alone converts the bistropolone meroterpenoid eupenifeldin into both ring-contracted phenolic products and carbon-retentive bridged polycycles, establishing a unified enzymatic origin for two structurally distinct natural-product scaffolds. Structure-guided mutagenesis uncovered a precisely organized electrostatic network that is critical for flavin-dependent oxygenation. Complementary well-tempered metadynamics simulations and quantum-chemical calculations support a Baeyer–Villiger branching mechanism, wherein the AO276 active site may preferentially stabilize alternative migration-competent conformations of a putative Criegee intermediate. Each conformation aligns a distinct C–C bond in an antiperiplanar geometry relative to the O–O bond; restricted conformational interconversion within the active site could preserve the initial reactive geometry and bias divergent carbon migration. Collectively, our findings identify conformational preorganization as a plausible contributor to regiodivergent enzymatic Baeyer–Villiger catalysis, offering a rational strategy for steering oxidative skeletal remodeling in complex natural product molecules.

title:
Tetrapyridophenazine-Based
Vinylene-Linked Covalent
Organic Frameworks for Efficient Sequential Photocatalysis and Continuous-Flow
Synthesis
content:
Abstract
Vinylene-linked covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are promising photocatalysts because their conjugated sp2-carbon frameworks combine exceptional chemical stability with efficient charge transport. However, the limited reversibility of C═C bond formation narrows the scope of polymerizable monomers, restricting the structural diversity and electronic tunability of vinylene-linked COFs. Here, we report a molecular design strategy based on a planar, electron-deficient, nitrogen-rich tetrapyridophenazine (TTPhz) building block for constructing vinylene-linked COFs. Knoevenagel polycondensation of a polymerizable TTPhz monomer with aromatic dialdehydes affords three highly crystalline COFs with tunable donor–acceptor interactions and electronic structures. The optimized fluorinated framework, TTPhz-COF-3, exhibits efficient charge separation and transport, enabling a previously unreported one-pot sequential photocatalytic synthesis of 2,3-dihydrobenzofuran derivatives from arylboronic acids through tandem aerobic hydroxylation and oxidative [3 + 2] cycloaddition. The catalyst displays broad substrate scope, excellent recyclability, and enables gram-scale continuous-flow synthesis of a key intermediate of the natural product (±)-conocarpan with a 4-fold higher turnover frequency than the corresponding batch process. This work expands the structural and functional scope of vinylene-linked COFs and establishes molecular building-block design as a general strategy for developing advanced crystalline organic photocatalysts.

title:
Multicomponent Nanocrystal
Superlattice Structure
Prediction from First-Principles Validated against Two Decades of
Experiments
content:
Abstract
Predicting nanocrystal (nanoparticle) assembly into ordered arrays (superlattices) is a grand challenge in materials chemistry that has largely resisted first-principles theories. Here, we extend MOLT-CF, a classical density functional theory, to multicomponent nanocrystal systems and subject it to a rigorous validation by comparing against nearly 300 experiments spanning two decades of literature. We use MOLT-CF to predict stability and phase diagrams for binary superlattices of nanocrystals with linear hydrocarbon ligands, as well as many other fine structural details, for example, lattice constants, packing fractions, ligand structure, and, in the case of (cubic) perovskite nanocrystals, orientation. Significant discrepancies from experiments are noted only for the Li3Bi and Cu3Au superlattices. In the former, we predict that this lattice is stabilized by particle fractionalization, which is supported by a reexamination of experimental data in the literature. In the case of Cu3Au (for which MOLT-CF predicts thermodynamic instability against phase separation into single-component lattices), we propose two alternative candidate structures that reconcile theory with experimental observations. These results establish MOLT-CF as a rigorous platform for the computational design of next-generation functional nanoparticle materials.

title:
Chemical
Bonding Rules for Stacking-Sequence Stability
in Bismuth Oxychloride Intergrowths and Their Consequences for Band
Structure
content:
Abstract
Metal oxyhalides are versatile materials, exhibiting properties relevant to photocatalysis, solid-state battery systems, ferromagnetism, multiferroics, and nonlinear optics. Here, mixed-metal oxyhalide intergrowths, layered materials formed by intercalating SrBi3O4Cl3 and Bi2GdO4Cl blocks along the c direction within a crystal, are reported. They are synthesized through a flux-based approach in which the SrBi3O4Cl3-to-Bi2GdO4Cl ratio can be precisely controlled. Despite the structural and compositional flexibility of such intergrowths, there is no general framework for predicting which local structural arrangements are preferred. Density functional theory combined with Bader charge analysis shows that preferred stacking sequences are those that minimize charge disproportionation across distinct chlorine environments, consistent with Pauling’s fifth rule, and we support this bonding-based framework through computational cation substitution that shifts the ionic-covalent balance of the metal–chloride bonding. With the preferred stacking arrangement established, this same system further reveals that intergrowth layering and Sr/Bi site occupancy modulate the interaction between the Bi3+ lone pair and anion p orbitals. Density functional theory calculations reveal that intergrowth formation destabilizes the O-2p orbitals, raising the valence band maximum for visible-light absorption, with the lone-pair interaction and layering-driven internal electrostatic field acting as competing effects on the resulting band gap. Significantly, this experimental-computational study establishes a transferable, bonding-based framework for stacking-sequence stability in layered oxyhalide intergrowths, while also clarifying how the same structural levers used to control stability can be tuned to engineer band structure.

title:
Direct Detection of
the Calcium–Sodium–Calcium
Metal Triad in Thermostable α-Amylases from  Bacillus sp.  Bacteria in Aqueous Solution by  23 Na Quadrupole-Central-Transition
NMR Spectroscopy
content:
Abstract
We report that the Na+ ion within the calcium–sodium–calcium (Ca–Na–Ca) metal triad in two thermostable bacterial α-amylases (ca. 58 kDa) can be directly detected by 23Na (I = 3/2) quadrupole-central-transition (QCT) NMR spectroscopy in aqueous solution. We show that 23Na QCT NMR signals from hyperthermostable Bacillus licheniformis α-amylase (BLA) and its mesophilic homologue, Bacillus amyloliquefaciens α-amylase (BAA), exhibit remarkable subppm spectral resolution, which is unprecedented in NMR studies of quadrupolar nuclei in proteins. Using this new 23Na QCT NMR methodology, we examine the pH-dependent unfolding, melting temperatures (Tm), long-term thermal inactivation profiles, and chemical denaturing of BAA and BLA. We also use 23Na QCT NMR to monitor EDTA titration experiments, which yielded the apparent binding constants of the Na+ ion to BAA and BLA to be (0.3 ± 0.1) × 109 and (0.6 ± 0.1) × 109 M–1, respectively. Because the Ca–Na–Ca metal triad is located in the vicinity of the active cleft, the subppm spectral resolution of 23Na QCT NMR makes it possible to detect subtle changes of the enzyme structure caused by the presence of inhibitors such as acarbose and quercetin. This work represents the first time that Na+ ions tightly bound to an enzyme are directly observed by 23Na QCT NMR in aqueous solution. This new 23Na QCT NMR approach can potentially be extended to detection of other metal ions with quadrupolar nuclei such as K+, Mg2+, and Zn2+ in metalloenzymes in their native aqueous environment.

title:
Redox
Properties of the Copper Centers in Particulate
Methane Monooxygenase
content:
Abstract
Particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO) and its homolog ammonia monooxygenase (AMO), central enzymes in the global carbon and nitrogen cycles, contain three highly conserved mononuclear copper centers, denoted CuB, CuC, and CuD. While these sites have been well characterized structurally and spectroscopically, with recent studies identifying CuD as the active site, their reduction potentials have not been measured. This knowledge gap has hindered efforts to determine how the two electrons and two protons required for substrate oxidation are sourced and delivered. Here, we have elucidated the redox properties of each copper center in pMMO/AMO by protein film voltammetry using samples with copper occupancies known from cryoelectron microscopy (cryoEM) structures. The reduction potential of the CuB site, −72 to −139 mV, is significantly lower than the ∼400 mV measured for the CuD site, with consistent values determined for pMMOs and AMO from different species. Mutation of a residue in the second sphere of CuB, Glu35, alters the redox potential and impairs cell growth and pMMO activity, indicating that redox chemistry at CuB might be functionally relevant. Finally, a Pourbaix diagram constructed for the CuBII/I and CuDII/I half-reactions suggests that a proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process occurs at the CuD site but not at the CuB site. Thermochemical analysis of this proposed PCET process is compatible with electron delivery by a quinol reductant. These results provide new context for future investigations of the pMMO and AMO reaction mechanisms.

title:
Clickable Photolabile
Linkers for Convenient Immobilization
and Light-Controlled Release of Substrates from Solid Support
content:
Abstract
Photolabile linkers (PLLs) enable spatiotemporal control over substrate release but often suffer from slow photorelease kinetics, low quantum yields, or limited functionalization options. Here, we report a family of heterobifunctional PLLs based on (3-hydroxy-5-alkoxynaphthalen-2-yl)methyl (NQMP) chromophores that combine rapid, high-yielding photochemical cleavage with orthogonal conjugation chemistries for efficient substrate immobilization and light-triggered release. Six heterobifunctional NQMP-based linkers bearing terminal acetylene, cyclooctyne, amine, carboxyl, allyl, and biotin groups were synthesized and employed for the immobilization of fluorescent dyes, acetylsalicylic acid, biotin, avidin, and doxorubicin on silica microspheres and mesoporous silica nanoparticles. Mild UV-A irradiation resulted in efficient release of the attached payloads while preserving the integrity of the solid support. Mesoporous silica nanoparticles provide high loading capacity and are suitable for light-controlled drug delivery. The modular design, excellent photochemical efficiency, orthogonal conjugation chemistries, and compatibility with diverse substrates make NQMP-based PLLs versatile tools for reversible surface functionalization, controlled cargo release, affinity capture, and photoresponsive drug delivery applications.

title:
Catalytic Asymmetric
1,6-Diene Cyclization via Designed
Carbocationic 5- and 6- exo  Pathways
content:
Abstract
Catalytic asymmetric electrophilic alkene functionalization provides a powerful strategy for the construction of complex chiral molecules. Despite significant progress in this field, the asymmetric functionalization of alkenes promoted by an electrophilic carbon species via an exo-cyclization mode remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report a solution to this challenge: alkenes can undergo designed 5-exo- and 6-exo-carbocationic cyclizations to generate optically pure, complex chiral compounds with high enantio- and diastereoselectivities. In this approach, for 1,6-dienes bearing bulky sulfonamide or quaternary carbon linkers, one double bond of the substrate interacts with an external electrophile, such as a trifluoromethylthio, arylthio, alkylthio, or chlorine species, generating an electrophilic carbon species that promotes the transformation of 1,6-dienes under chiral indane-based chalcogenide catalysis. Notably, the reaction can be terminated by intramolecular nucleophiles via cis-addition or can be captured by various intermolecular nucleophiles. A diverse array of optically pure polycyclic and monocyclic compounds can be obtained, including 5-5-6 tricyclic N-heterocycles and pentasubstituted chiral cyclohexanes. The same strategy can also be efficiently applied to 6-endo cyclizations, leading to the formation of 6-6-6 tricyclic and monocyclic N-heterocycles. The resulting products can be readily converted to various other valuable compounds, further demonstrating the utility of this methodology. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to rationalize the observed selectivities, revealing that the preferential transition-state conformations lower the activation barriers for the desired cyclization pathways. This work offers a versatile platform for the synthesis of enantioenriched chiral scaffolds prevalent in bioactive molecules and pharmaceuticals, significantly expanding the scope of polyene cyclization chemistry.

title:
Imaging of Electrochemically
Programmed Single-Molecule
Reactions
content:
Abstract
Single-molecule reactions reveal intrinsic heterogeneity that is obscured in ensemble measurements. However, most existing approaches rely on extreme dilution, ultrasmall solution volumes, or physical confinement to keep individual events sufficiently sparse. Here, we introduce electrochemically programmed single-molecule reactions (PSMR), a pulse-regulated strategy that shifts single-molecule electrochemistry from passive observation to active control. It converts continuous interfacial reactions to a sequence of short, repeatable reaction trials. By tailoring the pulse waveform, PSMR controls the driving force and duration of each reaction trial, thereby regulating the probability of single-molecule reactions, while the relaxation interval between pulses allows the interface to recover before the next trial. This coordinated control enables single-molecule reactions to be actively regulated under conventional solution volumes and reaction concentrations. By coupling individual reaction events to single-photon emission through electrogenerated chemiluminescence (ECL), we can directly count and image the reactions. The ultrashort reaction windows and relaxation periods suppress diffusion-layer buildup, thereby preserving sensitivity to local reaction kinetics, even at high overpotentials. Using this approach, individual Au nanoparticles were imaged over a broad potential range, and particles as small as 5 nm were distinguished from the substrate background. Sparse photon events were accumulated over repeated trials and further analyzed using localization- and fluctuation-based algorithms, enabling super-resolution mapping of reaction activity beyond the optical diffraction limit. PSMR therefore provides a framework for actively regulating, quantitatively imaging, and spatially mapping single-molecule electrochemical reactions at nanointerfaces, opening new opportunities for mechanistic studies and rational design across molecular electrochemistry, electrocatalysis, and energy conversion.

title:
Asymmetric Elongation
of Uranyl within a Silver Nanocluster
content:
Abstract
Confinement within nanoscale cavities can profoundly alter molecular structure and electronic properties, but this strategy has never been applied to inherently linear and symmetric uranyl cations (UO22+). Here, we report the first example of uranyl encapsulation within a self-assembled silver nanocluster, [UO2F5@Ag21(CCBut)14](BF4)3F (CCBut = 3,3-dimethyl-1-butynyl), abbreviated as UO2F5@Ag21. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals asymmetric elongation of the axial O ≡ U≡O bonds from the ideal symmetric value of 1.77 Å to 1.788(9) and 1.837(9) Å, respectively. Raman and IR spectroscopy show extreme redshifts of both symmetric and asymmetric stretching vibrations (ν1 down to 765 cm–1). Transient absorption spectroscopy further reveals an excited-state quenching process of the (UO2F5)3– guest driven by unique confinement. High-energy-resolved fluorescence detected X-ray absorption near edge structure (HERFD-XANES) at the U M4 edge demonstrates re-engineered 5f electronic states, with a shifted and broadened 5fσ* feature indicating reduced U≡O covalency. This work establishes nanoconfinement as a powerful new route to reshape the electronic structure and property of actinide-based materials.

title:
On-Surface Synthesis
of a Low Bandgap Cyclopenta[ c , d ]azulene-Based
Polymer
content:
Abstract
Nonbenzenoid topologies offer a compelling strategy to tailor the electronic properties of low-dimensional carbon materials. Here, we report the on-surface synthesis of a nonalternant polymer incorporating a [7–5–5] cyclopenta[c,d]azulene (CPA) motif on Au(111) via thermally induced Ullmann coupling. Bond-resolved scanning tunneling microscopy confirms the robustness of the [7–5–5] framework. Scanning tunneling spectroscopy, together with dI/dV mapping supported by density functional theory calculations, reveals a remarkable narrow polymeric bandgap of 1.5 eV. The electronic structure is governed by the intramolecular charge transfer from the heptagonal ring to the adjacent fused pentagonal rings, resulting in a pronounced dipole moment despite being composed exclusively of carbon and hydrogen. Aromaticity analyses indicate the coexistence of locally aromatic and slightly antiaromatic regions, highlighting the intrinsic electronic frustration associated with the nonalternant topology. These findings demonstrate how the controlled incorporation of [7–5–5] motifs enables the rational bandgap engineering in carbon-based polymers and expands the scope of nonbenzenoid design in on-surface synthesis.

title:
The
Molecular Logic of Platelet-Activating Factor
(PAF)
content:
Abstract
Platelet-activating factor (PAF) is a well-known if enigmatic lipid signal with important roles in inflammatory responses, allergic reactions, autoimmune diseases, and thrombotic cascades. Several lines of evidence suggest that our current model of PAF’s molecular mechanism is inadequate. This report describes a recontextualized model for PAF. The revised model embeds PAF in a plasmalogen-based molecular mechanism in which activation is a spontaneous chemical reaction triggered by environmental conditions that liberates a PAF receptor (PAF-R) agonist from a membrane-bound phospholipid. The active ligand subsequently undergoes a thermodynamically driven spontaneous rearrangement into an inactive isomer, a feature that controls response lifetime. The revised model is a molecule-autonomous set of transformations that create a response with spatial and temporal control. More generally the revised model’s congruence with a similar model for RORγt supports a picture in which plasmalogens form a part of the immune system that is separate from the cell-based innate and adaptive immune systems.

title:
Tailoring Superhydrophobic
Ultramicropores in Covalent
Organic Frameworks for Humidity-Resistant Methane Purification
content:
Abstract
Efficient purification of methane from raw natural gas under humid conditions remains challenging because water adsorption often degrades the separation performance and structural stability of porous adsorbents. Here we report a topology- and stacking-guided molecular design strategy that integrates ultramicropore engineering with pore-surface fluorination to construct superhydrophobic covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for humidity-resistant methane purification. Two isoreticular fluorinated COFs, TF-COF and NF-COF, were constructed by rationally controlling framework topology and interlayer stacking, generating well-defined ultramicropores for size-selective discrimination of C1–C3 hydrocarbons. Fluorination simultaneously enhances pore-wall hydrophobicity and strengthens host–guest interactions, creating a confined adsorption environment that promotes hydrocarbon recognition while effectively suppressing competitive water adsorption. As a result, NF-COF exhibits a propane uptake of 99.4 cm3 g–1 and an exceptional C3H8/CH4 IAST selectivity of 251.7 at 298 K. Dynamic breakthrough experiments further demonstrate efficient methane purification under both dry and highly humid conditions, with the separation performance fully retained at 97% relative humidity owing to its superhydrophobic surface. Theoretical calculations reveal that densely distributed fluorine atoms generate synergistic pore confinement and multiple C–H···F van der Waals interactions, simultaneously maximizing adsorption capacity and molecular discrimination. These findings establish fluorinated superhydrophobic COFs as a robust platform for energy-efficient natural gas upgrading under industrially relevant humid conditions.

title:
Unlocking the Tertiary
Nitrogen Effect in 3D Anisotropic
Covalent Organic Frameworks to Achieve Record Iodine Capture under
Industrial Conditions
content:
Abstract
Using porous adsorbents to achieve efficient capture of radioactive iodine from nuclear waste under industrial conditions remains a formidable challenge, since most adsorbents just exhibit a low iodine uptake under such conditions. We herein show two 3D [8 + 4]-assembled covalent organic frameworks (COFs, ECUT-COF-99 and ECUT-COF-100) for this challenging target. The two COFs feature a minimal-transitivity [3 4] flu-derived net, which allows anisotropic isoreticular expansion through a general sequential derived-net approach. ECUT-COF-100 was found to give an ultrahigh iodine uptake of 1.51 g/g under simulated industrial conditions (150 °C and 150 ppmv I2), 5.2-fold that of ECUT-COF-99 (0.29 g/g). Such performance also far exceeds all established organic adsorbents for this use. Mechanism studies reveal that nonaromatic tertiary nitrogen atoms allow for strong charge transfer from the lone-pair electrons of tertiary nitrogen to I2, leading to the formation of ionic iodides (I3– and I5–) and the N·+ radical cation and then fixing of ionic iodides by Coulomb interactions. This work not only provides a promising adsorbent with record iodine uptake for radioactive iodine capture from nuclear waste but also highlights a new insight into the tertiary nitrogen effect in 3D COFs for efficient iodine capture.

title:
Reactivity and Selectivity
of Photocatalytic Nitrate
Reduction Reaction to Ammonia: Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh Single Atoms on
p-Type TiO 2  Nanotubes
content:
Abstract
We present a systematic study of noble metal (Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh) single-atom cocatalysts decorated on p-type and quantum-confined TiO2 nanotubes for photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia. All single-atom cocatalysts were prepared through a reactive deposition using different metal precursors, resulting in a single-atom oxidation state (δ+) of δ ≈ 2. At a similar loading concentration (0.2–0.3 at%) and in the absence of any sacrificial agent, Pd single atoms exhibit the highest element-specific activity for ammonia production, while Pt single atoms display a prominent photocatalytic activity with a strong tendency of nitrite reduction toward ammonia. Rh single atoms achieve the highest ammonia selectivity, whereas Ir single atoms predominantly produce nitrite due to inhibited subsequent reduction. Comparisons with single atoms deposited on conventional TiO2 (P25) and with nanoparticles supported on the nanotubes reveal that both the semiconductor properties (quantum confinement effect and p-type conductivity) and the speciation of the cocatalyst (single atom) can significantly enhance activity and selectivity. These findings aid in establishing design principles for different single-atom catalysts toward efficient and selective photocatalytic nitrogen valorization.
