title:
Disentangling Modulator
and Fluoride Chemistry in
Rare-Earth Metal–Organic Framework Formation via Multinuclear
NMR Spectroscopy: A Mechanism-Guided Synthetic Redesign
content:
Abstract
Metal–organic framework (MOF) chemistry continues to expand, highlighting the need for molecular insight into framework formation. Solution-phase NMR provides a powerful, accessible, and economical means to probe these mechanisms. We examine the formation of rare-earth (RE) UiO-66, focusing on Yttrium(III)-UiO-66. RE-UiO-66 contains a hexa-metallic node in which the metals are bridged by μ3-fluorido, μ3-hydroxido, and/or μ3-oxido ligands, with benzenedicarboxylate linkers connecting nodes. The fluorido ligand derives from the α-fluorinated modulators required for this synthesis, yet its formation and incorporation pathways are unclear. Using in situ multinuclear NMR spectroscopy, we demonstrate that MOF formation proceeds via zero-order kinetics. Modulator is consumed approximately an order of magnitude faster than linker. The fluoride ligand is formed via nucleophilic aromatic substitution between modulator and in situ-generated dimethylamine. Mass balance suggests that the modulator plays a dual role, coordinating to the metal cation and generating fluoride. However, when solvent hydrolysis precedes MOF formation, the modulator acts primarily as a fluoride source; in situ-formed acetic acid acts as the modulator. Thus, the dual modulator role can be decoupled; benzoic acid functions as the modulator and tetramethylammonium fluoride serves as the fluoride source. Under these modified conditions, linker consumption is slow. When solvent hydrolysis precedes MOF formation, the reaction accelerates. This highlights the complex influence of acidity, competitive binding of fluoride, modulator, and linker on kinetically labile rare-earth metals. The tetramethylammonium fluoride procedure provides a versatile pathway to RE-UiO-66 derivatives (RE = Eu, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Yb, Lu) and two Y-UiO-67 derivatives.

title:
Accessing Syndiotactic
Alternating Poly(lactic- co -glycolic acid) via Dual
Regio- and Stereocontrol
content:
Abstract
Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) has attracted broad clinical attention for its exceptional biodegradability and biocompatibility. It is well established that the regio- and stereoregularity of PLGA has been shown to exert a significant influence on the material properties of the resulting PLGA. In this contribution, we report the design and synthesis of a class of readily tunable salalen aluminum complexes for regio- and stereoselective ROP of rac-MG. Ligand modification on this salalen system allowed us to access highly alternating and syndiotactic PLGA (Preg up to 98%; Pr up to 0.95 at 40 °C). The outstanding dual regio- and syndioselectivity has been exploited as an effective strategy for constructing a highly alternating copolymer P(MG-alt-EG) (Palt = 0.96). These findings manifested the beneficial effects of salalen Al complexes on regio- and stereocontrolled polymerization and represented an inspiring example to guide future catalyst design efforts.

title:
Kinetics
and Morphological Characteristics of Gas
Hydrate Formation in Methane–Water–Sand Particle Systems
content:
Abstract
Natural gas hydrates are considered one of the most important clean resources with great development potential. Numerous studies have focused on flow assurance problems resulting from hydrate formation in gas–water–oil systems of transportation pipelines. However, there have been limited investigations on morphological evolution and hydrate formation kinetics in complex multiphase gas–water–sand hydrate slurry systems for wellbore fluids during gas hydrate production, considering the influence of sand particles. This study explored gas hydrate morphological characteristics, formation kinetics, and deposition phenomena in different sand (quartz sand, muddy silt, and natural sand)–water slurry systems. Morphological results indicate two patterns of hydrate formation: the wall-adherent hydrate layer and the gas–liquid interfacial hydrate layer. The amount of sand particles in the hydrate layer adhering to the wall could increase with the sand particle concentration in slurry. The strong dispersion of muddy silt in slurry caused the different morphologies of the formed hydrate slurry from other sand systems, resulting in a wider distribution range of the hydrate layer adhering to the wall and a more uniform hydrate slurry. The morphology of the hydrate layer highly depended on the sand type. All three types of sand particles reduced the induction period of gas hydrate formation, accelerating hydrate growth. The most remarkable promoting impact on the formation kinetics of hydrates was found in the natural sand–water slurry due to the small-sized particles providing more hydrate nucleation sites. The muddy silt–water system provided the longest induction period for hydrate formation since more water bound in muddy silt particles hindered the mass transfer for hydrate formation.

title:
Electrostatic
and Microstructural Insights into Carbonate
Wettability under Activated Carbonated Brines with AOT Surfactant
content:
Abstract
This study introduces an integrated approach combining CO2, low-salinity carbonated brine, and sodium dioctyl sulfosuccinate (AOT) surfactant to systematically investigate their synergistic effects on the interfacial, electrostatic, and wettability characteristics of carbonate surfaces. The novelty lies in the concomitant investigation of interfacial, electrostatic, and microstructural analyses to clarify the underlying dominant mechanisms of wettability alteration in activated carbonated systems. The results showed that AOT significantly reduced IFT and accelerated relaxation time in the absence of CO2, particularly in seawater. However, CO2 dissolution increased IFT because of reduced interfacial activity, while simultaneously enhancing wettability alteration toward water-wet conditions. Contact angle and zeta potential analyses demonstrated that low-salinity carbonated brines with a low AOT concentration (50 ppm) achieved the strongest alteration in wettability (with a contact angle of approximately 24°) whereas no remarkable wettability reversal with contact angles of about 140° was observed at a high surfactant concentration (300 ppm) in seawater. Zeta potential analysis confirmed that low-salinity carbonated brines shifted the carbonate rock surface toward more negative values, enhancing electrostatic repulsion at the oil–brine–rock interface and promoting water-wet conditions. SEM and EDAX analyses further confirmed that surface morphology and elemental composition are strongly dependent on the brine–surfactant system. That is, low salinity promoted mineral dissolution and pore exposure, while high salinity and high surfactant concentrations caused surface coverage and reduced efficiency. The results provide a mechanistic basis for designing hybrid brine–surfactant–CO2 formulations for fractured carbonate reservoirs, particularly where wettability and interfacial properties are important controlling factors in fluid displacement.

title:
Review of
Sustainable Production of Biomass-Based
Amines Using Advanced Heterogeneous Nanocatalysis: Recent Trends and
Future Perspectives
content:
Abstract
Biomass-based amines are renewable precursors with versatile applications in pharma, agrochemical, food additive, lubricant, and polymer industries. Metal-based heterogeneous nanocatalysts have gained paramount importance for the synthesis of renewable amines due to their unique surface nanochemistry, tunable morphology, and cost-effectiveness, as well as their inherent acid-redox synergistic sites. The catalyst’s acid sites play a crucial role in C–N bond formation to generate reactive intermediates, whereas the redox sites accelerate the dissociative adsorption of hydrogen and the subsequent hydrogenation of intermediates to the targeted amines. This review focuses on the synthesis of renewable amines from nonedible lignocellulose-derived platform molecules, such as furfural (FAL)/its alcohol, 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF), levulinic acid (LA)/its esters, and vanillin, using various metal-based heterogeneous nanocatalysts. It provides a comprehensive discussion on the fundamental aspects of reagents’ activation, nanosize-dependent active-site design, structure–activity correlations, and mechanistic insights into the desirable functional renewable amines. Particular emphasis is placed on catalytic reductive amination and tandem C–N coupling strategies, with a critical evaluation of hydrogen adsorption/activation/spillover on the catalyst surfaces. Finally, it concludes with future perspectives for engineering next-generation heterogeneous catalysts for biomass valorization, while highlighting the catalytic production of novel bio-amines for the sustainable pharmaceutical industry, without relying on fossil-derived chemicals.

title:
Time-Resolved
Synchrotron-Based Investigation of Reactive
Pore Evolution in Sandstone for  CO  2  Storage
content:
Abstract
Understanding mineral dissolution in heterogeneous porous media is critical for predicting the evolution of subsurface systems during geological CO2 storage. Here, we integrate time-resolved synchrotron techniques, 4D X-ray microtomography (μ-CT), X-ray fluorescence (TR-XRF), and X-ray diffraction (TR-XRD) to investigate acid-induced dissolution in cemented sandstone from the Rio Bonito Formation in the Paraná Basin (South America) across multiple spatial scales. The results reveal that dissolution is strongly controlled by mineralogical heterogeneity and fluid accessibility, resulting in spatially localized, temporally evolving reaction fronts. Carbonate cement (calcite) dissolves rapidly under acidic conditions, as evidenced by a sharp depletion of the Ca signal (TR-XRF) and a continuous reduction in diffraction intensity (TR-XRD), driving early-stage porosity enhancement observed by μ-CT. In contrast, silicate phases (microcline) exhibit slower, surface-limited dissolution accompanied by partial structural modification, while quartz remains comparatively unreactive under the investigated conditions and experimental time frame. Dissolution rates show an exponential dependence on pH, confirming the dominant role of proton activity in controlling reaction kinetics. This behavior has direct implications for predicting injectivity evolution and geochemical buffering during the early stages of CO2 injection. Integrating structural, chemical, and mineralogical observations establishes a mechanistic link between phase-specific reactivity and pore-scale evolution. These findings highlight the importance of reservoir mineralogy, petrophysical properties, and diagenetic history in governing reactive transport processes. The results provide experimental constraints for reactive transport models addressing permeability evolution and early-stage geochemical alteration in CO2 storage systems.

title:
Mineralogical
and Microstructural Controls on the
Mechanical Weakening and Recovery of Longmaxi Formation Shale during
Flowback Fluid Soaking
content:
Abstract
During postfracturing shut-in, retained flowback fluid can alter the mineralogical, microstructural, and mechanical properties of deep shale. However, the links between these changes and fracture fractal characteristics during soaking remain poorly understood. Here, Longmaxi Formation shale was soaked in field-produced flowback fluid for 0–45 days and characterized using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, nanoindentation, Brazilian splitting, triaxial compression, micro-CT, and fractal analysis. The results reveal a nonmonotonic weakening and recovery process. The triaxial compressive strength decreased from 340.27 MPa in the unsoaked state to 256.92 MPa at 7 days, then recovered to 326.40 MPa at 30 days. Tensile strength decreased to 7.50 MPa at 15 days and increased to 10.74 MPa by 45 days. XRD and SEM results show time-dependent changes in mineral composition and surface morphology, together with the development of pores and microcracks and localized granular deposits. Nanoindentation further reveals strong spatial variations in elastic modulus and hardness during soaking. The line and surface fractal dimensions of Brazilian splitting fractures varied with fracture path tortuosity and tensile strength, whereas the CT-derived volumetric fractal dimension captured the evolution of triaxial fracture-network complexity with prolonged soaking. Overall, the results suggest early weakening associated with hydration and dissolution, followed by partial mechanical recovery associated with localized deposits and microstructural reorganization. These findings provide new insights into shale alteration, fracture evolution, and mechanical integrity during shut-in in deep shale gas reservoirs.

title:
Mechanical
Behavior of Layered Heterogeneous Hydrate-Bearing
Sediments: Insights from Triaxial Experiments and Numerical Modeling
content:
Abstract
The mechanical behavior of natural gas hydrate-bearing sediments (HBS) is critical for safe and efficient gas production. However, marine HBS commonly exhibit layered heterogeneity caused by spatial variations in clay distribution and hydrate saturation (Sh), whose effects on stress transfer and failure mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, triaxial shear tests were conducted on three types of heterogeneous HBS with a montmorillonite-bearing interlayer (HBShet-M), an illite-bearing interlayer (HBShet-I), and a low-hydrate-saturation interlayer (HBShet-Sh). An elastoplastic finite-element model based on the Mohr–Coulomb criterion was then established and validated against experimental results, with prediction errors of only 0.06–0.77% for failure strength (qf). The validated model was subsequently used to investigate the effects of layered heterogeneity on stress evolution and failure mechanisms during shearing. The results show that after inserting a clay interlayer into the middle layer, under σ3’ = 1 MPa, the peak deviatoric stress qf of HBShet-M and HBShet-I decreases by 3.65 and 4.05 MPa, respectively, compared with HBShom. Under high confining pressure, they decrease by 2.48 and 1.19 MPa, respectively. By contrast, HBShet-Sh reduces the strength of HBS by impairing hydrate cementation, with strength reductions of 5.14 and 5.03 MPa under low and high confining pressures, respectively. Preferential deformation of the weak layer governs failure in all heterogeneous HBS and induces pronounced stress concentration. The minimum and maximum principal stresses within the weak layer are 4.7–6.7 and 1.2–1.8 times those in the strong layer, respectively. These findings provide new insights into the failure mechanisms of layered heterogeneous HBS and offer theoretical guidance for safe marine gas hydrate production.

title:
Multifractal
Evolution Characteristics of Multiscale
Fracture-Pore Structures in Coal under CO 2  Phase-Transition
Fracturing
content:
Abstract
To deeply analyze the multifractal evolutionary characteristics of multiscale fracture-pore structures in coal subjected to CO2 phase transition fracturing (CO2–PTF), CO2–PTF experiments on coal samples were carried out in this study. Multiple multiscale fracture-pore characterization techniques, including computed tomography (CT) scanning, high-pressure mercury intrusion (HPMI), low-temperature N2 adsorption (LTNA), and low-temperature CO2 adsorption (LTCA), were adopted to systematically investigate the variations in fracture-pore structural parameters of coal after CO2–PTF treatment. Moreover, classical multifractal theory was introduced to explore the multifractal responses of the fracture–macropore–mesopore–micropore system in CO2–PTF coal, and to uncover the evolution of local heterogeneity within the multiscale fracture-pore structural system. The results indicate that CO2–PTF induces fracture generation and expansion-transformation effects in coal, causing the volume, surface area, and maximum length of the fractures in coal to increase significantly by 2626.55%, 833.12%, and 115.93%, respectively. This leads to a pronounced increase in the heterogeneity of fracture distribution across low-probability, high-probability, and overall zones. For macropore–mesopore structures, CO2–PTF has a pore enlargement-conversion effect, which enhances the heterogeneity of macropore distribution in low-probability, high-probability, and overall zones, yet reduces the heterogeneity of mesopore distribution over these three regions. Notably, CO2–PTF imposes no obvious transformation effect on micropore structures, which arises from the chemical properties of micropores. Such chemical characteristics of micropores limit the effective transformation and stimulation of coal reservoirs via CO2–PTF. Accordingly, future studies should focus on green chemical stimulation technologies for coal reservoirs.

title: Overcoming Indium-Tin-Oxide Optical Losses in InAs Colloidal Quantum-Dot Light-Emitting Diodes at 1550 nm
content:
Abstract
Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) based on colloidal InAs quantum dots (QDs) have emerged as promising light sources for the short-wave infrared (SWIR) range. However, their development is limited by relatively low photoluminescence quantum yield as well as intrinsic device design challenges. Here, we report LEDs with electroluminescence (EL) in the SWIR based on InAs/ZnSe core/shell colloidal QDs, synthesized via a seedless one-pot approach that enables the rapid growth of relatively large InAs cores. Zirconium-doped indium oxide (InZrO) was used as the bottom transparent electrode owing to its significantly higher infrared transparency compared to the commonly employed tin-doped indium oxide (ITO). These two key innovations pushed the EL beyond 1500 nm, with external quantum efficiencies of 3.0, 1.2, and 0.6% at 1093, 1198, and 1547 nm, respectively.

title: Pressure-Driven Topological Reconfiguration toward Fast-Charging Hard Carbon with Plateau-Capacity Retention
content:
Abstract
Conventional carbonization of semi-coke induces excessive ordering of aromatic skeletons, producing dense graphitic structures that hinder Na+ intercalation and suppress low-potential plateau capacity. Here, we develop a rapid thermomechanical coupling sintering strategy using moderate pressure to drive π–π interactions and topological reconfiguration of aromatic units. This process suppresses excessive graphitization while constructing interconnected, twisted pseudo-graphitic domains with abundant closed nanopores. At 1000 mA g–1, PTR-HC reaches 80% SOC in ≈14.4 min and retains 90.1% of its plateau capacity, enabled by abundant Na+ storage sites and rapid diffusion pathways. Kinetic analyses reveal accelerated Na+ transport and a thin, NaF-rich solid-electrolyte interphase with fewer organic components. In situ XRD and Raman attribute slope capacity to surface/defect adsorption and intercalation and the plateau capacity to quasi-metallic Na clusters in closed pores. This work establishes pressure-driven topological engineering as a promising strategy for upgrading semi-coke into fast-charging hard carbon with high plateau-capacity retention.

title: Vacuum-Evaporated Molecules with Giant Spontaneous Orientation Polarization for Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
Abstract
Interfacial losses at the perovskite/C60 and C60/metal contacts limit inverted perovskite solar cell performance. Here, we introduce a vacuum-evaporated molecule with giant spontaneous orientation polarization, 6F-2PI, for simultaneously tailoring both interfaces. Incorporating 6F-2PI increases the work function of perovskite, reducing the conduction band offset at the perovskite/C60 interface, which facilitates electron extraction. Concurrently, its phthalimide moieties passivate defect states, suppressing nonradiative recombination, as evidenced by a 0.03 eV recovery in quasi-Fermi level splitting. At the C60/metal interface, 6F-2PI also delivers efficient charge extraction, improved interfacial contact, and thermal resilience. Moreover, its hydrophobic fluorinated units prevent moisture ingress. Consequently, this dual-interface modulation boosts PCE from 18.5% to 22.5% with exceptional device stability, retaining over 90% of its initial efficiency after 2000 h under ambient conditions. Furthermore, this framework exhibits universal compatibility across both vacuum-deposited and solution-processed devices and simplifies processing for mass production.

title: Grain Boundary Character Governs Lithium Deposition Uniformity on Polycrystalline Copper
content:
Abstract
In anode-free Li metal batteries, a bare current collector must be converted into a reversible Li metal anode during the first charge, making Li nucleation decisive for reversibility. However, how current collector microstructure governs Li nucleation and growth remains poorly understood, since prior studies focused on single-crystal surfaces to identify favorable crystallographic orientations, leaving grain boundaries unexplored. Here, we identify grain boundary density and character in copper current collectors as key regulators of Li deposition uniformity. Systematic annealing decouples grain size from surface chemistry, revealing that deposition uniformity improves with copper grain coarsening but saturates as disordered boundaries are eliminated during grain growth, leaving predominantly low-energy configurations. Atomistic simulations show disordered boundaries impose high barriers to Li adatom migration, whereas ordered boundaries and adjacent low-index terraces provide low-barrier pathways for redistribution. Copper foils engineered beyond this threshold sustain uniform Li plating across diverse electrolytes and improve cyclability in anode-free cells.

title: Fabrication of Multicavity Hierarchically Porous Carbon Nanospheres Using Compressed CO 2  for Overall Water Splitting
content:
Abstract
The rational design of efficient bifunctional electrocatalysts is crucial for overall water splitting. As a catalyst support, the multicavity hierarchically porous carbon spheres scaffold facilitates efficient electron transport and structural stability during catalysis. Herein, we report a reverse microemulsion strategy assisted by supercritical/compressed CO2 for the synthesis of multicavity hierarchically porous carbon nanospheres. Pyrolysis of nickel phthalocyanine (NiPc) and dicyandiamide as nickel and nitrogen sources, respectively, yields nickel nanoparticles embedded in nitrogen-doped porous carbon nanospheres modified with atomically dispersed Ni sites (Ni–N@MC). The multicavity hierarchically porous structure affords abundant active sites and an enlarged interface, exhibiting low overpotentials of 197 mV for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and 148 mV for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at 10 mA cm–2, thus demonstrating excellent bifunctional electrocatalytic activity. An overall water-splitting electrolyzer using this catalyst as both electrodes achieves 10 mA cm–2 at 1.59 V with over 24 h stability.

title: RuO 2 -Modified High-Entropy Spinel Electrocatalysts for Efficient Alkaline Water-Splitting Reactions
content:
Abstract
Developing cost-effective electrocatalysts that can efficiently and stably drive alkaline water-splitting is crucial to the large-scale production of hydrogen. Herein, high- and medium-entropy spinel materials, (CoCuFeMnNi)3O4 (HESOx), (CoCuFeMnNi)3O4PVP (HESOxPVP), and (CoFeMnNi)3O4PVP (MESOxPVP) are prepared via the reverse coprecipitation method and calcination and modified with RuO2 for enhanced performance. The RuO2-modified HESOxPVP exhibits enhanced HER performance, requiring an overpotential of 24.3 mV to achieve 10 mA cm–2. In addition, RuO2/(CoCuFeMnNi)3O4PVP (RuO2/HESOxPVP) shows better OER, reaching 10 mA cm–2 at 322 mV overpotential. Two electrode water-splitting tests with the RuO2/HESOxPVP as both anode and cathode attained 10 mA cm–2 at 1.36 V. It also shows good tolerance toward long-term activity, thereby showing promise as a potential electrocatalyst for large-scale production of hydrogen and oxygen via water-splitting.

title: Decoupling Carrier Concentration and Mobility in Hot-Extruded n-Type Bismuth Telluride for Enhanced Thermoelectric Performance
content:
Abstract
Bi2Te3-based materials have attracted considerable attention due to their excellent thermoelectric performance at room temperature. However, the pulverization process during fabrication tends to introduce the donor-like effect, which significantly increases the carrier concentration and consequently degrades the room-temperature thermoelectric properties, especially for n-type Bi2Te3-based materials. In this study, decoupling of carrier concentration and mobility was achieved by a two-step heat treatment combined with hot extrusion. During the pre-annealing process, Te vacancies were introduced into the lattice by controlling Te volatilization, and Bi atoms migrated into these vacancies, generating holes and thereby reducing the carrier concentration. The post-annealing temperature exhibited a negligible influence on the carrier concentration but substantially improved the carrier mobility. The hot-extruded Bi2Te2.8Se0.2 sample with a two-step treatment achieved the optimized carrier concentration and the enhanced mobility. As a result, a maximum zT of 1.13 was achieved at 350 K, marking a nearly 40% enhancement compared with the directly extruded sample. This performance substantially exceeds the typical values reported for n-type Bi2Te3-based materials via other processing routes, demonstrating that our strategy offers an effective route to decouple carrier concentration and mobility and thereby enhance thermoelectric performance. This work thus provides a practical and scalable pathway for waste-heat recovery and near-room-temperature cooling applications.

title: Three‐in‐One Spacer Strategy Toward Highly Alkali‐Resistant Covalent Organic Frameworks for Efficient Oxygen Evolution Reaction in Alkaline Seawater
content:
An alkali‐resistant phthalocyanine‐based COF catalyst (CoPc‐NH‐TABQ‐iAA) is developed by a three‐in‐one spacer strategy, which endows CoPc‐NH‐TABQ‐iAA with high alkaline resistance, high atomic utilization and effective mass transfer. CoPc‐NH‐TABQ‐iAA shows an ultra‐low overpotential of 77 mV and a long‐term durability of 290 h at 500 mA cm−2 in 6 M KOH and seawater at 80°C in AEM electrolyzer.








ABSTRACT
Molecular catalysts with well‐defined active sites and structural tunability are proposed as promising electrocatalysts for alkaline oxygen evolution reaction (OER). However, poor alkaline resistance, low atomic utilization, limited mass transfer resulted in rapid activity degradation and unstable catalytic performance of molecular catalysts in alkaline environments. Herein, a three‐in‐one spacer strategy was designed to develop highly alkali‐resistant phthalocyanine‐based covalent organic frameworks (COFs) by integrating a spacer with hydrophilic groups and stable piperazine linkages in skeletons, which endows COF with high alkaline resistance, high atomic utilization and effective mass transfer. As a result, the COF shows a surprising activity with an ultra‐low overpotential of 77 mV and a long‐term durability of exceeding 290 h at 500 mA cm−2 in 6 M KOH and seawater at 80°C in an anion exchange membrane electrolyzer. To the best of our knowledge, the unprecedented stability and activity exceeds all organic catalysts. Theoretical and experimental studies reveal that the hydrophilic units not only increase the mass transfer, but also can facilitate the *OH deprotonation on the Co sites, which further improve the catalytic activity.

title: Exploring Local Structure in Iron Oxide Nanoparticles During Chemical Vapor Synthesis by in Situ and Operando X‐Ray Absorption Spectroscopy
content:
In situ and operando XAS is used to probe nanoparticle formation during chemical vapor synthesis, where particles form in the gas phase under high‐temperature conditions. XANES reveals dynamic changes to the oxidation states while EXAFS indicates local structural variations under in situ probing conditions. Mean square displacements may allow estimation of particle temperatures.








ABSTRACT
Early stages of nanoparticle (NP) formation in gas‐phase synthesis processes, such as chemical vapor synthesis (CVS), involve (trans‐)formations of molecular species (precursors), small clusters (nuclei), or amorphous intermediates before forming the final NP product. These transformations may be probed using in situ and operando X‐ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), enabling the observation of local structure evolution under CVS conditions. However, this is challenging due to the very dilute sample system, that is, NPs in the gas phase, coupled with high temperatures required for particle formation, deteriorating the signal‐to‐noise ratio. Here, we present an experimental setup specially tailored to overcome these challenges, enabling in situ and operando XAS measurements of sufficient quality to perform quantitative data analysis. The major focus is a comprehensive understanding of the formation of iron oxide NPs in CVS. Quantitative XANES analysis reveals controlled changes of oxidation states of iron under varying oxygen partial pressures, while EXAFS analysis using reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) simulations provides detailed insight into local structure around the iron atom probed as a function of process temperatures. The mean square displacements available from RMC analysis may be used to estimate the temperature of NPs in the gas phase or to determine their Debye temperatures.
